interactive.brief: The one thing you should see is each end of the row of marchers slowing as it crosses into the water, so the row and the ray turn towards the normal, when you drag the ray's angle.
interactive.title: The boundary
interactive.whatAmILookingAt: A short lesson in fourteen small screens on light crossing the flat surface of water or glass, seen from the side. Some screens show an idea and the rest ask you to try it. Air is at the top and a block of water or glass is below. A ray of light strikes the surface. It is a straight line with an arrow, and you can drag its angle. Where it strikes, a thin line stands at 90° to the surface. That is the normal. Every angle is measured from it and labelled. The ray carries on into the block, bent. A faint second ray reflects off the surface. By the law of reflection, it leaves at the angle the ray arrives. Readouts show the angle of incidence, the angle of refraction and sin i ÷ sin r. A switch swaps the block between water and glass. Water's index is 1.333. Glass is given an index of 1.50 for the examples. Here is the rule the picture follows. Light is slower in water and glass than in air. A marchers switch draws the light's front as a row of marchers. The end that crosses first slows first, so the row turns. A ray entering a slower material turns towards the normal. A ray leaving it turns away. How far is set by n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r. Here n is each material's refractive index. It is light's speed in empty space divided by its speed there. Air's index is taken as 1. A reverse switch sends the ray from inside the block out into the air. Dragged to the critical angle, the bent ray lies along the surface. Dragged past it, the bent ray vanishes and all the light reflects. A prism mode sends white light through a triangle of glass. An apparent-depth mode draws a coin in a tank with an eye above it. The eye is always drawn. So are the rays from the coin to the eye and the dashed lines traced straight back from the eye. A readout that would give a puzzle's answer shows "?" until the answer is checked. Any row of readouts wraps onto two lines on a phone. The screens, in order. Screen 1, do, The coin in the tank: a tank of water seen from the side, a coin on its floor, an eye above and to one side, and a rod held beside the eye and pushed along its line of sight at where the coin looks. "You see a coin in a tank and push a rod straight at it. The rod misses. Where is the coin really?" Choices, in a column: Deeper than it looks (right); Just where it looks; Nearer the surface than it looks; Off to one side, at the depth it looks. Hint on Just where it looks: "Then the rod would have hit it. The light changed direction on its way to your eye." Hint on Nearer the surface than it looks: "The rod followed your line of sight. It passed over the coin." Hint on Off to one side, at the depth it looks: "The bend at the surface also changes how deep the coin seems." Read: "A coin lies in a tank of water. You push a rod straight at where it looks. The rod misses. Where is the coin really?" Why: light from the coin bends as it leaves the water. Your eye traces it straight back, to a point above the real coin. So the coin is deeper than it looks. After Check the ray from the coin to the eye appears, bent at the surface, with its dashed line back to where the coin seems to be. Screen 2, show, Slower means a bend: a ray from the air into water, the normal, both angles and the faint reflected ray. Words: "Light travels more slowly in water than in air. Picture its front as a row of marchers. The end that reaches the water first slows first. So the row swings round towards the normal." Then "Drag the ray, and switch the marchers off and on." Read: "A ray meets water at 40° to the normal and carries on at 28.8°. Each end of its row of marchers slows as it crosses. So the row turns towards the normal. A faint ray reflects at 40°." The screen opens with the marchers on, walking in. Still: the ray at 40° with the marchers on. Screen 3, do, Square on: a ray pointing straight down the normal at the water. "A ray strikes the water square on, along the normal. What does it do?" Choices, in a column: Goes straight on, more slowly (right); Bends to one side; Goes straight on at the same speed; All of it reflects back. Hint on Bends to one side: "Both ends of the row reach the water together." Hint on Goes straight on at the same speed: "It is in water now. Light is slower in water." Hint on All of it reflects back: "Most of it goes in. Only a little reflects." Read: "A ray strikes the water square on, along the normal. What does it do?" Why: both ends of the marchers' row reach the water at the same moment. They slow together, so the row does not turn. The light still slows. After Check the marchers cross square on. Screen 4, show, The index: the ray entering water, with the material switch. Words: "The refractive index, n, says how much slower light is. It is light's speed in empty space, 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s, divided by its speed in the material. Fresh water's is 1.333. So light crosses water at 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.333 = 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s. Air's is so near 1 that we take it as 1. Glass is taken as 1.50 here." Then "Swap the material." Read: "Glass is given an index of 1.50 here. It slows light more than water does. So it bends the ray further towards the normal." Still: water. Screen 5, do, typed, Find the index: a glass block with the light's two speeds labelled and its index showing "?". "Light travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in empty space and 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a glass block. What is the glass's refractive index?" A typed answer: 1.50, to two decimal places, with no unit. Slips: 0.67, "That is upside down. Divide the speed in empty space by the speed in the glass."; 1.33, "That is water's index. Work it out from this glass's speed." Hint: "Index = speed in empty space ÷ speed in the material." Read: "Light travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s in empty space and 2.00 × 10⁸ m/s in a glass block. What is the glass's refractive index?" Why: 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 2.00 × 10⁸ = 1.50. An index has no unit. It is one speed divided by another. The index shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 6, show, Snell's law: the ray from the air into water, with the sin i ÷ sin r readout. Words: "Snell's law says how far the ray bends: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r. Both angles are measured from the normal. From air into water at 40°, sin r = sin 40° ÷ 1.333 = 0.643 ÷ 1.333 = 0.482. So r = 28.8°. Snell's law goes past GCSE." Then "Drag the ray." Read: "As the ray turns, both angles change. But sin i ÷ sin r stays at 1.333 for water. At 40°, the ray carries on at 28.8°." Still: the ray at 40°. Screen 7, do, typed, Into glass: a ray from the air meeting glass at 50° to the normal, the angle of refraction showing "?". "Light goes from air into glass of index 1.50, at 50° to the normal. What is the angle of refraction?" A typed answer: 30.7°, to one decimal place. Slips: 33.3°, "Divide the sine of the angle, not the angle itself."; 59.3°, "That is measured from the surface. Give it from the normal."; 50°, "The ray bends as it enters. Light slows in glass." Hint: "Divide sin 50° by the glass's index. Then find the angle." Read: "Light goes from air into glass of index 1.50, at 50° to the normal. What is the angle of refraction?" Why: sin r = sin 50° ÷ 1.50 = 0.766 ÷ 1.50 = 0.511. So r = 30.7°. The angle shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 8, show, Why the coin looks higher: the apparent-depth mode, a coin 1.2 m down in a tank, an eye above, the rays from the coin and their dashed lines back. Words: "Light from the coin bends away from the normal as it leaves the water. Your eye traces it straight back, to a point above the coin. Looking nearly straight down, the angles are small. The two depths are in the ratio of the angles' tans. A small angle's tan is almost its sine. So the depths are in the ratio of the sines, 1 ÷ n. The coin looks to be at its depth ÷ n. A tank 1.2 m deep looks 1.2 ÷ 1.333 = 0.90 m deep." Then "Drag the eye." Read: "Wherever the eye is, its traced-back rays meet nearer the surface than the real coin. From straight above, a coin 1.2 m down looks 0.90 m down." Still: the eye straight above the coin. Screen 9, do, typed, How deep?: the coin on the floor of a tank, 0.60 m down, the eye straight above, the depth it looks showing "?". "A coin lies 0.60 m down in fresh water. Looking straight down, how deep does it look?" A typed answer: 0.45 m, to two decimal places. Slips: 0.80 m, "Water makes things look shallower. Divide by the index. Do not multiply."; 0.60 m, "That is its real depth. The light bends as it leaves, so the coin looks shallower." Hint: "Divide the real depth by water's index." Read: "A coin lies 0.60 m down in fresh water. Looking straight down, how deep does it look?" Why: 0.60 ÷ 1.333 = 0.45 m. The depth shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 10, show, The way out: the reverse switch on, the ray inside the water heading up to the air. Words: "Going from water out into air, light bends away from the normal. So sin i ÷ sin r turns upside down, to 1 ÷ 1.333 = 0.750. At the critical angle, c, the bent ray lies along the surface, at 90°. For water, sin c = 1 ÷ 1.333, so c = 48.6°. Past it, sin r = 1.333 × sin i would be above 1. No angle has that sine. So no light gets out, and all of it reflects. The critical angle goes past GCSE." Then "Drag the ray past the critical angle." Read: "Inside water, a ray at 48.6° to the normal leaves along the surface. Past 48.6°, all the light reflects back into the water." Past the critical angle the full reflection and its label fade in. Still: the ray just past 48.6°. Screen 11, do, typed, Glass's critical angle: a ray inside a glass block heading up to the air, the bent ray along the surface, the angle inside showing "?". "This one goes past GCSE. What is the critical angle for light going from glass of index 1.50 out into air?" A typed answer: 41.8°, to one decimal place. Slips: 48.6°, "That is water's. Use the glass's index, 1.50."; 48.2°, "That is measured from the surface. Give it from the normal." Hint: "At the critical angle the bent ray is at 90°. So sin c = 1 ÷ 1.50." Read: "This one goes past GCSE. What is the critical angle for light going from glass of index 1.50 out into air?" Why: n₁ sin c = n₂ sin 90°, so 1.50 × sin c = 1 × 1. That gives sin c = 0.667. So c = 41.8°. The angle shows "?" until the answer is checked. Screen 12, show, A prism: the prism mode, a narrow beam of white light entering one sloping face of a glass triangle. Words: "A prism is a block of glass with sloping faces. Glass's index is a little higher for violet light than for red. So violet bends most at each face. White light fans out into colours." Read: "White light enters a glass prism and leaves as a fan of colours. Red is bent least and violet most." Still: the prism mode. Screen 13, do, mixed, A water prism: a glass prism with a 45° corner turning light through 90°, beside a thin-walled prism of the same shape filled with water. "A glass prism with a 45° corner can turn light through 90°. Inside, the light meets the long face at 45°, and all of it reflects. Would a thin-walled prism filled with water do the same?" Choices, in a column: No, 45° is under water's critical angle (right); Yes, any 45° prism reflects all of it; Yes, water bends light more than glass; No, water reflects no light at all. Hint on Yes, any 45° prism reflects all of it: "All of it reflects only past the critical angle. Compare 45° with water's." Hint on Yes, water bends light more than glass: "Water's index is lower than glass's. So it bends light less." Hint on No, water reflects no light at all: "Water reflects some light. The question is whether all of it reflects." Read: "A glass prism with a 45° corner can turn light through 90°. Inside, the light meets the long face at 45°, and all of it reflects. Would a thin-walled prism filled with water do the same?" Why: glass's critical angle is 41.8°, under 45°. So in glass the light reflects completely. Water's is 48.6°, more than 45°. So at 45° much of the light gets out through the long face. Two glass prisms can stand in for a periscope's two mirrors. Binoculars fold their light with prisms in the same way. After Check the light leaks out through the water prism's long face. Screen 14, do, mixed, typed, Water into glass: a ray in water striking a glass block at 30° to the normal, the angle in the glass showing "?". "Light in water strikes a glass block at 30° to the normal. Water's index is 1.333 and the glass's is 1.50. What is the angle of refraction in the glass?" A typed answer: 26.4°, to one decimal place. Slips: 19.5°, "The light starts in water, not air. Multiply sin 30° by 1.333 first."; 34.2°, "The indexes are swapped. Light slows going into glass, so it bends towards the normal." Hint: "Use n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r, with n₁ = 1.333 and n₂ = 1.50." Read: "Light in water strikes a glass block at 30° to the normal. Water's index is 1.333 and the glass's is 1.50. What is the angle of refraction in the glass?" Why: 1.333 × sin 30° = 1.333 × 0.5 = 0.667. Then sin r = 0.667 ÷ 1.50 = 0.444. So r = 26.4°. The angle shows "?" until the answer is checked.
interactive.ignores: Light is drawn as rays, thin straight lines. The marchers are a picture of slowing. Light as a wave, with its wavelength, is left out. The surfaces are perfectly flat and clean. The faint reflected ray only marks where some light goes. How much reflects really changes with the angle. Air is given an index of exactly 1. Light is really very slightly slower in air than in empty space. Each material has one index, except in the prism mode. Really every index shifts a little with colour and with temperature. Sea water's index is a little higher than fresh water's. Lenses and curved surfaces are left out. Glass's index of 1.50 and every angle and depth are example figures.

explain.text:
Light bends where it crosses into water or glass because it changes speed there. Snell's law links the angles on each side. It says how much the light bends.

Light is slower in water than in air. Picture its front as a row of marchers. Meet the water at a slant, and one end crosses first and slows first. The other end still moves at the faster speed. So the row swings round towards the normal. A ray entering a slower material bends towards the normal. A ray leaving it bends away. Square on, both ends slow together. So the ray goes straight on, just more slowly.

The [[refractive index]], n, measures the slowing. It is light's speed in empty space divided by its speed in the material.[^3] Light in empty space travels at 3.00 × 10⁸ m/s. Fresh water's index is 1.333.[^2] So light crosses water at 3.00 × 10⁸ ÷ 1.333 = 2.25 × 10⁸ m/s. You know this kind of ratio from cable fault location. A cable's velocity factor is a pulse's speed in the cable divided by the speed in empty space. It is the same kind of ratio, turned over.

Snell's law gives the angles: n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r. Here i is the angle of incidence and r is the angle of refraction. Both are measured from the normal. Coming in from air, n₁ is taken as 1. Then the index is simply sin i ÷ sin r. From air into water at 40°, sin r = sin 40° ÷ 1.333 = 0.643 ÷ 1.333 = 0.482. So r = 28.8°.

Now go the other way, from water out into air. The angle outside is the larger one. At the [[critical angle]] it reaches 90°, and the bent ray lies along the surface.[^4] Put sin 90° = 1 into the law, and sin c = n₂ ÷ n₁. For water into air, sin c = 1 ÷ 1.333 = 0.750, so c = 48.6°. Past that angle, sin r = 1.333 × sin i would be above 1. No angle has a sine above 1. So no light leaves, and all of it reflects back inside. That is [[total internal reflection]]. It cannot happen going into a slower material. There sin r is always smaller than sin i.

The same rule explains why a coin in water looks too high. Its light bends away from the normal as it leaves the water. Your eye traces it straight back, to a point above the coin. Looking nearly straight down, the angles are small. A small angle's sine and tangent are almost equal. Light can run either way along a ray. So name the angles as for light coming in: i in the air, r in the water. A ray leaves the surface a small sideways step from straight above the coin. Going down to the coin, that step is the real depth × tan r. Traced back from the eye, it is the apparent depth × tan i. So the apparent depth is the real depth × tan r ÷ tan i. That is almost exactly the real depth × sin r ÷ sin i, which is the real depth ÷ n. So a tank 1.2 m deep looks 1.2 ÷ 1.333 = 0.90 m deep.

Glass's index is a little higher for violet light than for red. So a prism's sloping faces bend violet most and fan white light into colours. All this is a teaching model, with rays, flat surfaces and one index for each material. Real indexes also shift a little with temperature. **Light bends at the edge of water or glass because it changes speed there, and n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r says by how much.**

analogy.text: Push a sack barrow at a slant from smooth concrete onto soft grass. One wheel reaches the grass first and drags. The other still rolls freely on the concrete. So the barrow swings round to cross the edge more squarely. Once both wheels are on the grass it runs straight again, just slower. Push it square on, and both wheels slow together, so it does not turn. Light's front turns at a boundary in the same way. It turns towards the normal as it slows.
analogy.breaks: The barrow turns because its wheels are joined by an axle and the grass drags on one of them. Light has no axle. Each part of its front simply travels at the speed of the material it is in. Light's bend is set by the two indexes and the angle it arrives at.

practice.text:
- Never look into the end of a live optical fibre or along a laser beam. Water and glass can bend a beam where you do not expect it.
- Draw the surface. Mark the normal where the ray strikes.
- Measure both angles from the normal. If you are given the angle to the surface, take it from 90°.
- Decide which way it bends. Into a slower material with a higher index, it bends towards the normal. Out into a faster one, it bends away.
- Write n₁ sin i = n₂ sin r and put in what you know. Find the missing sine, then take the inverse sine.
- If the sine you need comes out above 1, no ray gets out. All the light reflects.
- Something in water looks shallower from straight above. Divide its depth by the index to find how deep it looks.

**Rule of thumb:** looking straight down, things in fresh water look 1 ÷ 1.333 = 0.75 of their real depth. That is about three quarters. Water's critical angle into air is 48.6°. Glass's is lower, so glass traps light more easily.

**Worked example:** a spanner lies on the floor of a fresh-water tank 1.2 m deep. From straight above, it looks 1.2 ÷ 1.333 = 0.90 m down. So reach 1.2 − 0.90 = 0.30 m deeper than it looks. From the side it looks shallower still.

**Where you meet it:** an optical fibre keeps its light in by total internal reflection. Its core has a higher index than the glass around it. So light striking the wall at a glancing angle reflects completely.

**Common mistakes**
- Measuring the angles from the surface instead of the normal.
- Dividing the angle by the index instead of its sine.
- Writing the index upside down, as the speed in the material over the speed in empty space.
- Leaving out n₁ when the light starts in water or glass, not air.
- Expecting total internal reflection on the way into a slower material.
- Aiming at where a thing in water looks to be.
